title: The Boy Who Looked at Life From the Gene's Point of View
author: Richard Dawkins
wiifm: Why do people help strangers, cheat partners, sacrifice for their children and cooperate with rivals? The Selfish Gene gave a generation of readers a single lens for all of it, and the surprising part is that it ends up explaining kindness as well as selfishness. You will follow Richard Dawkins from a farm childhood in colonial Africa to Oxford in a winter of power cuts, where he wrote a book that changed how we see ourselves, and you will learn the strategy for cooperation that his book made famous.

b: Clinton Richard Dawkins was born on the twenty-sixth of March 1941 in Nairobi, Kenya. His father, Clinton John Dawkins, was an agricultural civil servant in the British colonial service, and both his parents were keen amateur naturalists. The boy spent his early years in Kenya and in Nyasaland, now Malawi, among birds, insects and the endless question of why living things are shaped the way they are.

The family returned to England in 1949, when he was eight, and settled on a farm in Northamptonshire. He went to Oundle School and grew up a fairly ordinary Anglican. In his mid-teens, as he later told it, he began to find the argument from design unconvincing, and once he understood Darwin's idea of natural selection properly, he felt he no longer needed a designer to explain life at all.

Hold on to that moment. Dawkins's whole career has been an attempt to make other people feel what he felt then: that natural selection is not one theory among many but an explanation of breathtaking power, able to account for the eye, the wing and, as it turned out, the strange mixture of selfishness and generosity in human beings.
ch.cap: Young Richard chases butterflies under Kenyan acacias

b: Dawkins went up to Balliol College, Oxford, in 1959 to read zoology. There he came under the influence of Niko Tinbergen, the Dutch scientist who would share a Nobel Prize in 1973 for founding the study of animal behaviour. Tinbergen supervised Dawkins's doctorate, on how young chicks make choices when they peck, and taught him to ask four kinds of question about any behaviour, including the crucial one: what is it for, in evolutionary terms?

After a spell teaching at the University of California, Berkeley, in the late 1960s, Dawkins returned to Oxford in 1970 as a lecturer. Meanwhile something important was happening in evolutionary biology. A handful of thinkers, above all William Hamilton, George Williams, John Maynard Smith and Robert Trivers, had worked out new mathematics showing that much of animal behaviour made sense only when you asked what it did for genes, not for the individual animal or the species.

Their central move was to reject a popular and comfortable idea, that animals do things for the good of the species. George Williams, in his 1966 book Adaptation and Natural Selection, argued that this was almost always wrong. A lemming does not throw itself off a cliff to save its species, and the famous film footage of lemmings doing so was staged for a Disney documentary in 1958. A creature that sacrificed itself for strangers would leave fewer offspring, and its sacrificing tendency would die out. So if animals help each other, there must be another explanation.

Their papers were dense and technical. Dawkins saw that the ideas inside them were thrilling, that almost nobody outside a small circle understood them, and that they changed the answer to the question every human eventually asks: why am I like this?
ch.cap: Dawkins records chicks pecking under Tinbergen's eye

b: Dawkins started writing in 1972, during a period of strikes and power cuts in Britain, when he could not get on with laboratory work. He put the manuscript aside, then picked it up again in 1975 and finished it. Oxford University Press published The Selfish Gene in 1976, when he was thirty-five.

The title was a deliberate provocation and it has been misunderstood ever since. Dawkins did not mean that genes have feelings or motives, or that people are bound to be selfish. He meant something more precise. Genes that build bodies which make more copies of those genes become more common. Genes that do not, disappear. So, looking back, it is as if genes were striving to be copied, and that useful as if is a metaphor for a purely mechanical process.

He later said he could equally have called it The Immortal Gene, or The Cooperative Gene, and that either would have been accurate. But the provocative title sold it, and arguably it also set off a long trail of confusion that he spent decades correcting.

The book was an immediate success with general readers and a talking point among scientists. Its clarity was part of the point. Dawkins wrote for an intelligent reader with no biology, explaining difficult mathematics through stories about birds, bees and imaginary computer games, and that style became a model for a whole generation of popular science writers.
ch.cap: Dawkins types The Selfish Gene during a power cut

b: Dawkins begins at the very beginning, in the primeval soup of the early earth. At some point, by accident, a molecule formed that could make copies of itself. He calls it a replicator. Copying was not perfect, so there were variations, and the variations that copied faster, or lasted longer, or copied more accurately became more common. Natural selection had begun before anything was alive in the ordinary sense.

Over billions of years, replicators that built protective structures around themselves did better. Those structures became cells, then bodies. Dawkins's arresting phrase is that we are survival machines, robot vehicles blindly programmed to preserve the selfish molecules known as genes. A chicken, in an old joke he enjoys, is just an egg's way of making another egg.

The point is the shift in viewpoint. A body dies, and in sexual reproduction its unique combination of genes is shuffled and lost. But an individual gene can be copied, nearly perfectly, for millions of years, passing from body to body like a baton. So if you want to understand why a behaviour exists, ask what it did for the genes that built the body doing it.

Dawkins pushed the idea further in his second book, The Extended Phenotype, in 1982, which he considers his most important. A gene's effects, he argued, do not stop at the skin. A beaver's dam is as much a product of beaver genes as its teeth are, and a parasite's genes can reach out and change the behaviour of its host. Genes are best understood by everything they do in the world, not just the bodies they build.
ch.cap: The first replicator copies itself in the primeval soup

ch.h: Why your genes make you kind
b: Here is the twist that makes the book far more hopeful than its title. If genes are what get copied, then a gene for helping your relatives can spread, because your relatives are likely to carry copies of the same gene.

This was William Hamilton's insight, published in 1964 and usually called kin selection. A full brother shares on average half of your genes by descent, a cousin about an eighth. So a gene that made you willing to take a risk for a sibling could prosper even if it sometimes cost you your life. The biologist J B S Haldane is said to have quipped years earlier that he would lay down his life for two brothers or eight cousins, though the exact story is told in several versions.

Dawkins illustrates the logic with a thought experiment he named the green beard effect. Imagine a gene that did three things at once: gave its carrier a green beard, made it notice green beards on others, and made it kind to them. Such a gene could spread by favouring copies of itself in strangers. Dawkins thought this was unlikely in practice, because a single gene doing all three things is improbable, though biologists have since found a few real cases, including in fire ants.

Kin selection explains the devotion of parents, the sterility of worker bees who serve their sisters, and the warmth most of us feel towards family. It also explains conflict. Robert Trivers showed that parents and children have partly different genetic interests, which is why a toddler demands more than a parent wants to give, and why weaning can be a battle.

Trivers also explained why the sexes often behave differently. In his theory of parental investment, the sex that puts more into each offspring, usually the female with her large egg and often pregnancy and care, becomes choosier about mates, while the sex that invests less competes harder for access. Dawkins called his chapter on this the battle of the sexes. The pattern is a tendency, not a law, and it reverses in species like seahorses, where males carry the young.
ch.cap: A man wades in for two brothers as cousins watch

b: Dawkins then borrowed an idea from his friend John Maynard Smith: the evolutionarily stable strategy. Imagine a population where animals fight over food. Some play hawk and always fight hard. Some play dove and always back down. Which wins?

The answer is neither, outright. In a world of doves, a hawk does brilliantly because nobody resists. But in a world of hawks, everyone gets badly hurt, and a dove who walks away does better. The population settles into a stable mixture, where no individual could do better by switching strategy. Nobody planned it. It simply emerges from the arithmetic of costs and rewards.

This way of thinking, borrowed from game theory, was one of the most valuable things Dawkins brought to a general audience. It shows how behaviour in a group can settle into patterns that no individual chose and that are hard to shift, which is something anyone who has watched a market, an office or a family will recognise.
ch.cap: Two hawks fight over food as a dove walks away

b: The deepest puzzle is cooperation between strangers who are not related. For this Dawkins drew on Robert Trivers's theory of reciprocal altruism, and in the second edition of the book, published in 1989, he added a famous chapter called Nice Guys Finish First.

It tells the story of the political scientist Robert Axelrod, who around 1980 ran computer tournaments of a game called the prisoner's dilemma. Two players each choose to cooperate or betray. Betrayal pays best if the other cooperates, but if both betray, both lose. Experts submitted strategies, and they played each other many times. The winner was the simplest entry, submitted by the psychologist Anatol Rapoport. It was called Tit for Tat. Cooperate on the first move, then copy whatever the other player did last time.

Tit for Tat is nice, because it never betrays first. It is retaliatory, because it punishes betrayal at once. It is forgiving, because it returns to cooperation as soon as the other does. And it is clear, so others quickly learn that cooperating with it pays. Dawkins's point is that selfish genes can produce genuinely cooperative creatures, because in a world of repeated encounters, cooperation is often the winning strategy.

Dawkins describes a striking real example from the First World War, which Axelrod also discussed: the live and let live system in the trenches. In some quiet sectors, opposing units facing each other for months developed unspoken truces, firing predictably or harmlessly, because each side knew the other would respond in kind. High command disliked it and broke it up by ordering raids that ended the repeated, predictable contact.
ch.cap: Trench soldiers fire high in a silent truce

b: In the final chapter of the 1976 book, Dawkins did something that took on a life of its own. He suggested that genes may not be the only replicators. Ideas, tunes, catchphrases, fashions and ways of making pots also copy themselves, jumping from brain to brain by imitation. He called these units of culture memes, from a Greek root meaning imitation, shortened to rhyme with gene.

He offered the idea almost playfully, to show that Darwinian thinking need not be tied to DNA. The word spread far beyond biology, and today it mostly means a funny picture shared online, which amuses him. As a scientific programme, memetics has struggled; critics argue that ideas change too much as they pass between minds to behave like genes, and the field never produced the rigorous results its fans hoped for.

But the core point is useful. Ideas compete for attention and survival, and the ones that spread are not necessarily the truest, only the best at being copied. Anyone who has watched a rumour outrun a correction knows exactly what he meant.

He also offers the idea of a meme complex, a cluster of ideas that survive better together than apart, much as genes cooperate within a body. A religion, a political movement or a company culture can be seen this way, with beliefs, rituals and stories that protect one another from challenge.
ch.cap: A catchy tune leaps from head to head

b: The Selfish Gene was attacked from the start. Some critics, including the philosopher Mary Midgley, thought the language of selfishness smuggled in a bleak view of human nature. Others, like the biologist Stephen Jay Gould, argued that it focused too narrowly on genes and ignored the role of whole organisms, development and chance. A long and continuing debate, revived by E O Wilson and others, has asked whether selection can also act meaningfully on groups.

Most evolutionary biologists still find the gene's eye view powerful and broadly correct, but they treat it as one useful perspective among several rather than the whole story. Modern work on how genes are switched on and off, and how environments shape development, has made the picture richer and messier than a simple selfish replicator.

Dawkins himself always insisted that the book was a description of how nature works, not a guide to how we should behave. In a line near the end he says that we, alone on earth, can rebel against the tyranny of the selfish replicators. That is the real message. Understanding where our impulses come from is the first step to choosing which ones to follow.
ch.cap: A man snips the strings tying him to his genes

b: Dawkins went on to become Oxford's first Charles Simonyi Professor for the Public Understanding of Science in 1995, and later one of the most famous critics of religion in the world. But The Selfish Gene remains his most influential book, still selling decades later and voted in a Royal Society poll in 2017 the most inspiring science book of all time.

In 2006 a thirtieth anniversary edition appeared, and in 2016 a fortieth. In his later introductions Dawkins kept returning to the same frustration: readers who judged the book by its title and assumed it was a manifesto for greed. People who actually read it, he noted, tend to come away with the opposite impression, that the cold mechanics of evolution can produce warmth, loyalty and fair play.

Its gift is a change of angle. Look at a parent, a rival, a colleague or a customer, and ask what strategy is being played and what it pays off. Often the answer explains behaviour that looked irrational. And then remember the twist: the same cold arithmetic that produces selfishness also produces loyalty, generosity and cooperation, especially between people who expect to meet again.
ch.cap: Dawkins holds up his book before a helix of people

take: Cooperation wins when encounters repeat. Treat every client, supplier and colleague as someone you will meet again, because in business you usually will.
Be nice, but not a pushover
Tit for Tat never betrays first, responds to betrayal at once and forgives quickly. Open with good faith, set clear consequences and do not hold grudges.
Strategies win when others can quickly read them. Make your terms, standards and responses easy to understand so people learn that cooperating with you pays.
Behaviour that seems irrational often makes sense once you ask who benefits. Before judging a person or a market, map what each player gains.
Hawk and dove mixes settle without anyone choosing them. Expect group habits in a team or industry to snap back unless you change the payoffs.
Memes win by being easy to repeat, not by being true. Make your important messages simple and memorable, and check catchy claims before passing them on.
Dawkins insisted nature's logic is not a moral guide. Knowing why you feel an impulse gives you the power to choose whether to follow it.
recall: What did Dawkins mean by calling genes selfish?

He meant that genes which build bodies that copy them become more common, so it looks as if genes strive to be copied. It is a metaphor for a mechanical process, not a claim that genes or people have selfish motives.
How does kin selection explain kindness?

Relatives share genes, so a gene that leads you to help a sibling or child can spread through their success. William Hamilton worked out the mathematics in 1964, explaining parental care and the self-sacrifice of worker insects.
What is an evolutionarily stable strategy?

It is a pattern of behaviour that, once common in a population, cannot be beaten by any alternative. In the hawk and dove example, the population settles into a stable mix where no individual gains by switching.
Why did Tit for Tat win Axelrod's tournaments?

It cooperated first, retaliated immediately against betrayal, forgave as soon as the other cooperated, and was simple enough for others to read. This showed that cooperation can win in repeated encounters even among self-interested players.
What is a meme in Dawkins's original sense, and how has the idea fared?
A meme is a unit of culture, such as a tune or idea, that copies itself by imitation. The word caught on hugely, but memetics as a science has struggled because ideas change too much in transmission.
note: Dawkins's childhood, Tinbergen supervision and the writing during the power cuts of the early 1970s come from his memoir An Appetite for Wonder. The Nice Guys Finish First chapter was added in the 1989 second edition, drawing on Axelrod's tournaments. The Haldane quip about brothers and cousins is widely repeated but exists in several versions. Debates over group selection and the limits of the gene's eye view, raised by Gould, Midgley, E O Wilson and others, continue.
words: Describing animals, objects or processes as if they had human feelings and intentions.
Dawkins's selfish gene is a deliberate anthropomorphism: genes have no motives, but it helps to talk as if they were striving to be copied.
Explaining something by the purpose or goal it seems to serve.
Natural selection produces things that look designed for a purpose, and Dawkins's whole career has been showing that no designer or teleology is needed.
The observable traits of a living thing, produced by its genes acting in its environment.
In The Extended Phenotype, Dawkins argued that a beaver's dam is as much part of its phenotype as its teeth.
Existing at or from the very beginning of time or of a process.
Dawkins's story begins with the first replicator forming by accident in the primordial soup of the early earth.
The practice of exchanging help or favours with others for mutual benefit.
Robert Trivers's reciprocal altruism, and Tit for Tat's success in Axelrod's tournaments, show how reciprocity lets unrelated strangers cooperate.
stories: Everyone knows lemmings hurl themselves off cliffs to save their species from overcrowding. Biologists in the 1960s, led by George Williams, argued that this sort of thing almost never happens: an animal that sacrificed itself for strangers would leave fewer young, and the habit would die out. So where did the famous image come from? From a Disney nature documentary released in 1958, White Wilderness, in which the lemming plunge was staged by the film makers. The world's most famous example of animals acting for the good of the species was manufactured. Dawkins built The Selfish Gene on the realisation that the comfortable idea was wrong.

Around 1980 the political scientist Robert Axelrod invited experts to submit computer strategies for the prisoner's dilemma, a game where two players choose to cooperate or betray, again and again. Game theorists sent in clever, devious programs. The winner was the shortest one, sent in by the psychologist Anatol Rapoport: Tit for Tat. Cooperate on the first move, then copy whatever the other player did last time. It never betrayed first, punished betrayal at once and forgave as soon as the other side came back. Dawkins added the story to his 1989 edition under the chapter title Nice Guys Finish First, his proof that selfish genes can build cooperative creatures.

In parts of the First World War's trenches, the same units faced each other across no man's land for months. In some quiet sectors, without a word being signed, a system grew up that historians call live and let live. Shelling came at predictable times and places, rifle fire went harmlessly high, and each side held back because the other would answer in kind. It was Tit for Tat played with real lives, and Axelrod and Dawkins both used it as an example. High command hated it. Their fix was to order raids that broke the repeated, predictable contact, and once the game stopped repeating, the cooperation collapsed.
biz: Play Tit for Tat with lenders and partners

Your lenders and introducers deal with you again and again, which is exactly where Axelrod found cooperation wins. Be nice first: send cases that are complete, accurately described and suitable for that lender's criteria, so they learn that cooperating with you pays. Be clear: put your standards in writing, such as how fast you return documents. If a partner lets you down, raise it promptly and specifically once, then go back to normal when they put it right. This week, track two numbers per lender: the share of cases accepted first time, and days from submission to decision. Improve your side of both.
Make the true message the catchy one

Memes spread because they are easy to copy, not because they are true. People in debt meet a lot of catchy, misleading claims about writing debts off, and some arrive at Debt Support Direct believing them. You cannot out-shout them with fine print, so make the honest message just as memorable. This week, write one short, accurate line for each brand that a client could repeat to their partner, for example what Debt Support Direct actually does and that advice is free. Use it in ads, on WhatsApp and on calls. Measure how many callers can say back correctly what happens next.
connects: Munger's insistence on asking who benefits matches Dawkins's habit of explaining strange behaviour by asking what it pays the genes.
Hawk and dove mixtures that settle without anyone choosing them are the kind of self-stabilising feedback Meadows describes in systems of every sort.
Voss's negotiation advice and Tit for Tat share the insight that in repeated dealings, opening with good faith and responding clearly to bad faith earns the best long-run results.
recap:
Begin in colonial Africa in the nineteen forties, with a small boy called Richard Dawkins, the son of two keen amateur naturalists, surrounded by birds and insects and the question of why living things are shaped the way they are. The family moves to a farm in England when he is eight. In his teens he decides that the argument from design does not convince him, and that Darwin's idea of natural selection explains life without any designer at all. His whole career is an attempt to make other people feel that thrill.

At Oxford he studies under Niko Tinbergen, a future Nobel winner, and he watches a handful of biologists quietly overturn an old comfort: the idea that animals do things for the good of the species. They argue it is almost always wrong. A creature that sacrificed itself for strangers would leave fewer young. Even the famous film of lemmings leaping off a cliff was staged.

In nineteen seventy two, with strikes and power cuts stopping his lab work, Dawkins starts writing. The Selfish Gene comes out in nineteen seventy six.

The first big idea is a change of viewpoint. Bodies die, but genes are copied for millions of years. We are survival machines, built by genes that happened to be good at getting copied. Selfish is a metaphor, not a motive.

The second idea is the twist that makes the book hopeful. A gene for helping your relatives can spread, because your relatives share your genes. That explains a parent's devotion and the worker bee serving her sisters.

The third is that behaviour in a group settles into stable patterns that nobody planned, like a mixture of fighters and peacemakers where neither can do better by switching.

The fourth is the most useful of all. In a famous computer tournament, the winning strategy was Tit for Tat. Cooperate first, copy what the other player did last time, punish betrayal at once, forgive quickly. When people expect to meet again, nice guys finish first.

The fifth is the meme, an idea that copies itself from mind to mind, and wins by being catchy rather than true.

Critics said the book was too narrow, or too bleak, and the debate about genes and groups goes on. But Dawkins always insisted that he was describing nature, not telling us how to behave. We alone, he wrote, can rebel against our selfish replicators.

Here is the line to remember: the same cold arithmetic that produces selfishness also produces loyalty and fair play, especially between people who expect to meet again.
